newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Goodyear strike deepens rubber market gloom.
newsitem.headline: Goodyear strike deepens rubber market gloom.

text.p: Asian rubber traders reacted glumly on Tuesday to a strike at leading U.S. tyre maker Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., saying the dispute will put further pressure on prices in an already depressed market.

Goodyear resumed limited production at nine strikebound plants on Monday, in an effort to keep tyre supplies flowing to automakers, as negotiators attempted to resolve the dispute over a new three-year labour contract.
About 13,000 members of the United Steelworkers of America walked off their jobs just after midnight on Sunday in the first strike in 21 years at the largest U.S. tyre maker.

"The situation is getting worse and worse. We are already frustrated because buyers are scarce and now this strike happens. We are just wondering what's next," said one trader in Indonesia, which exports the bulk of its rubber to the U.S.
A trader in Singapore estimated Goodyear's consumption of rubber at around 300,000 tonnes a year.
"One month, you lose 25,000 tonnes," he said.
"If it lasts only a few weeks, it will not have an impact. If it goes on more than a month, it will have a significant impact," the trader added.
Another dealer said extended industrial action at Goodyear could spook Southeast Asian rubber producers into selling more supplies into the market on fears already weak prices have further to fall.

Indonesian natural rubber prices had slipped to around 47 U.S. cents a lb FOB on Tuesday, from 48 cents on Monday, and local traders said they expect them to decline to 45 cents within a matter of days.
"The strike has led to the postponement of shipment contracts until the problem is settled. As a consequence, rubber is abundant but there are few buyers," one said.

The Goodyear strike is not initially expected to have a direct impact on Japanese rubber futures markets which list Thai benchmark RSS rubber rather than the SIR (Standard Indonesian Rubber) generally purchased by the U.S. tyre maker.
But if Southeast Asian cash rubber markets continue to fall then this could feed through into already bearish Japanese futures in Tokyo and Kobe.
Traders said the price of Standard Malaysian Rubber (SMR) has fallen by about 6.0 percent in the last six months to an average of 315 Malaysian/Singapore cents a kg.

They said it will be difficult for Malaysian rubber factories and growers to sustain their businesses if the price -- a weighted average of the Singapore and Malaysian currencies -- dips below 300 cents.
Malaysian rubber industry officials blame the market's predicament on a price squeeze exerted by European, Far East and U.S. importers, who consume most of the rubber produced by the country.
These importers, who act for manufacturers of tyres, gloves, condoms and other rubber products, persistently try to buy below production costs, the officials said.
Competition from cheaper Indonesian rubber is also eating into Malaysian sales, they added.

Malaysian Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik warned recently that without "fair and remunerative prices", rubber growers will be forced to cut back on production "and prices will spiral like nobody's business".
But U.S. and European tyre-makers with representative offices in Singapore said rubber prices were dictated by market forces and that they were not engaged in manipulation.
